description:
We are Bebrateam, a team of second-year students from Cherkasy State Technological University, specializing in Cybersecurity and Information Protection.

We are passionate about technology, programming, cybersecurity, and space exploration. Our goal is to develop an innovative solution using NASA data and modern digital technologies to address a real-world challenge.
summary: Burning Calendar harmonizes NASA’s two active fire records, MODIS (since 2000, 1 km pixels) and VIIRS (since 2012, 375 m pixels), into one consistent history of burning activity. The sensors cannot be compared directly: VIIRS detects about 3.1 times more points for the same fires, so 2012 looks like a fire surge when only the satellite changed. We place hotspots on a common ~10 km grid, count each fire cell once per day, merge both satellites after 2012 and correct MODIS before 2012 with a monthly coefficient. The result is one continuous series for 2000–2025. Our web app lets emergency managers, scientists and land managers choose an area and years, then see a burning calendar heatmap, a hotspot map, an early-warning level for any date against past years, anomalies and critical periods, and download Excel or CSV. For Ukraine we show seasonal peaks, unusual years and a switch that separates frontline regions. It turns raw hotspots into a trustworthy baseline for early warning.
details:
What it does. Burning Calendar is a web application that turns MODIS and VIIRS active fire hotspots from NASA FIRMS into one harmonized burning activity calendar. The user selects an area of interest and a range of years (2000–2025) and instantly sees when it usually burns, which years were unusual and what is happening now.

The problem. MODIS (Terra and Aqua, since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) have different pixel sizes, sensitivity and overpass times. In our data VIIRS gives about 3.1 times more points than MODIS for the same fires, so adding raw points makes 2012 look like a sharp increase in fires. MODIS is nearing the end of its life, so a consistent record is needed for the transition.

How we harmonize.

  1. We put all hotspots on a common grid of about 10 km.
  2. A cell with at least one detection in a day counts as one “burning center”, regardless of how many points fell in it. This removes the pixel-size effect.
  3. After January 2012 we take everything that at least one satellite detected (union of both).
  4. Before 2012 we multiply MODIS by a monthly coefficient k = union / MODIS, estimated on the years when both satellites operate (from about ×2.3 to ×8.5 depending on the month).

This gives one continuous series. For Ukraine the raw 1.6 million points become about 1.0 million aligned burning centers, with an average of 40 thousand per year.

What the app shows. Calendar heatmap (a row per year, a cell per week or month), hotspot map with seasonal filters, early warning (alert level for any date and window compared with the same days in other years, plus the usual change over the next 4 weeks), critical periods, anomalies, a MODIS vs VIIRS tab that proves why harmonization is needed, a methodology tab, and download of Excel and CSV. Users can filter by data source and point reliability, and exclude frontline regions from 24.02.2022.

Findings for Ukraine (2000–2025). Two burning seasons: March–April (spring burning) and July–September; 2008 is the hottest year (about 2.0 times a normal year). Examples built into early warning: Chornobyl zone, April 2020, and Ukraine, March 2015.

Benefits and impact. Responders get a consistent baseline to compare the current month with the historical median, scientists get a fair 25-year series, and land managers can plan monitoring for critical periods. The method works for any area.

Tools. Python, Streamlit and Plotly for the web app and charts, pandas for processing ; NASA FIRMS data. The grid and coefficient approach was designed by the team.

Team. Bebrateam, second-year Cybersecurity students at Cherkasy State Technological University. Roles: data processing, data quality checks against real events, app testing.

Use of AI. An AI assistant (Claude) was used to help prepare the presentation text and layout . No AI-generated images or video are used; all visuals are screenshots of our app. No NASA logos or branding are used.

Video walkthrough of the app: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1vZ1m8qqWr5sv1h-NBAPVDt2ReAgVs7zN/view?usp=drive_link, https://drive.google.com/file/d/1qhfw_nRZoZDbhKqSzwMT9jH8HmwY2jch/view?usp=drive_link
